author: Neil Rackham
biz: Replace closing attempts with an agreed next step

Rackham's clearest finding is that pressure helps small decisions and damages large ones. A secured loan against a family home is about as large as a household decision gets, so any urgency in your phone and WhatsApp scripts is working against you as well as against Consumer Duty. This week, go through the call guides and strike every urgency line, then give every adviser one defined advance to ask for instead, such as a call back at a time the customer chooses. Measure the share of calls ending with a customer agreed next step, and watch your drop out rate after documents are issued.
Use implication questions to understand, never to amplify

Implication questions work by making a cost visible, which is honest with a comfortable borrower and harmful with a frightened one. For Debt Support Direct, write a two line rule this week: implication questions are for establishing the facts of the situation, and the moment a client shows distress the adviser moves to listening and to what support is available, with no product talk in that call. Measure it by sampling recorded calls for a vulnerability flag being raised and the adviser pausing, and track complaints and withdrawals against the sampled calls.

b: Neil Rackham was born in England and spent part of his childhood in Borneo. Almost nothing else about those years sits on the public record. What is documented is where he came ashore: Totton Grammar School in Hampshire, then the University of Sheffield, where he took a degree in psychology in 1966.

He stayed on at Sheffield as a research fellow until 1969, and the work he did there decided the rest of his life. His job was to build tools that could measure interpersonal skills, not describe them. How do you put a number on the way one person negotiates with another, or sells to them?

The method was called behaviour analysis, and it is brutally simple. You sit in the room, listen to every single thing said, and drop each utterance into a category: that was a proposal, that a request for information, that a disagreement. At the end you have a tally sheet, and two trained observers watching the same meeting should produce nearly the same one, or the categories are no good.

What the method refuses to do is the interesting part. It will not let you say a meeting had a poor atmosphere or a salesman lacked charisma. Those are opinions wearing a lab coat. It only lets you say that one person made four proposals and another eleven, and that one pattern went with better outcomes more often.
Out of those years came three books on management training and interactive skills, read by almost nobody, and all of them practice for the thing he had not yet thought of doing.

b: The idea arrived the way good research questions usually do, which is sideways, from somebody else, in conversation. A colleague pointed out that in most sales forces the best tenth of salespeople sold roughly three times what the worst tenth sold. Then came the sentence that did the damage: nobody knows why.

Here was a profession with an enormous, stable, repeatable performance gap, measured every month in every company in the world, and no reliable account of what caused it. There were thousands of accounts filling the training rooms, and hardly any had been tested against what successful people actually said in front of customers.

From 1970 to 1974 Rackham was managing director of a firm called Performance Improvement Limited, which put him inside the training industry. By his own description what was taught was not good. American methods were being exported to Europe at the point when they had already stopped working in America. One widely taught course recommended about twenty short closes in a single sale. Another advised salespeople not to ask questions, on the reasoning that a question gives the customer an opening to voice a doubt.

That last piece of advice is worth sitting with, because it tells you the model of the human being underneath. The customer is a container of objections. Your job is to keep the lid on and ask for the order until fatigue does the rest.

In 1974 he founded the Huthwaite Research Group. He did not set out to write a sales book. He set out to answer the three to one question with the only instrument he trusted: a tally sheet and a very large number of real conversations.

b: Research of that kind costs money, and nobody funds a study that might conclude their training department has wasted the budget for a decade. Rackham's way in was an argument with a flattering edge. The methods taught in Europe, he said, were built on American customer psychology. Europe might need a model of its own, and would anyone care to find out what it was?

Xerox said yes. By Rackham's account the company had a surplus it needed to spend and a reputation as one of the best sales organisations in the world, which meant it had something to protect. Other multinationals followed, among them IBM, and the funding reached about one million dollars.

What the money bought was people in rooms. Over roughly twelve years, around thirty researchers sat in on about thirty five thousand sales calls, made by more than ten thousand salespeople, in more than twenty countries. They were not asking salespeople afterwards what they thought they did, a method that produces beautiful fiction. They sat in the corner and coded each utterance as it happened.

Rackham went in with a confident hypothesis and watched it die. He expected the Scandinavians to sell one way and the southern Europeans another, and had promised his funders a distinctly European model. Across thirteen countries at Xerox, the successful salespeople were doing the same things as each other, and the unsuccessful ones making the same mistakes as each other.

That is a bigger result than the one he was hired to produce. If success in a sales conversation has a shape that survives language and culture, it is not a personality trait and not a knack. It is a sequence of behaviours, and behaviours can be counted, taught and learned.
ch.cap: Selling a study to the people being studied

b: Every trade has a holy relic, and in selling it was the close. The assumptive close, where you write the order as though it were agreed. The alternative close, where you ask whether they want delivery on Tuesday or Thursday, a choice between two yeses. Trainers taught these as the decisive moment: more closes, more orders.

The tally sheets said something else, clearly enough that Rackham spent years being disbelieved. In small, cheap, quickly decided sales, closing techniques did raise success rates. In large sales, the more closing techniques a salesperson used, the worse that call did.

The cleanest demonstration came from a company selling both inexpensive items and expensive ones to the same customers. Its people were trained in closing. Sales of the cheap products went up and sales of the expensive products went down. The same technique, applied by the same people in the same week, helped one half of the business and damaged the other.

The explanation is not mysterious once you look at the buyer rather than the seller. Pressure works when a decision is small enough to regret cheaply. Now make it a commitment you must defend to a finance director, a spouse or a board in six months time. Someone applying pressure to that decision is not helping you decide. They are giving you a reason to delay, because the pressure itself is evidence that the seller's interest and yours have come apart.

Rackham did not conclude that asking for commitment was wrong. He concluded that an industry had spent fifty years perfecting the end of the conversation without checking whether the end was where sales were won.
ch.cap: The sacred technique, held up to the light

b: Before you can study a sales call you have to say where you are in one. Rackham's four stages are so plain their usefulness is easy to miss. The preliminaries, the opening warm up. Investigating, where the seller finds out about the buyer. Demonstrating capability. And obtaining commitment, where the call ends in something or nothing.

The preliminaries mattered far less than the training industry believed. Opening benefit statements, the polished first sentence, the studied rapport: in large sales these made very little difference, which is embarrassing, since they are the part most people rehearse.

The deeper correction was to the word success. A call can end in four ways. An order, where the customer buys. An advance, where the customer agrees to a specific action that moves the sale forward: a site visit, a trial, a date in a diary. A continuation, where the sale does not move but the door stays open. Or a no sale.

The continuation is the quiet killer. It is the call that ends with the customer saying this has been very interesting, do send me some information, ring me in a few weeks. It feels like progress and produces a cheerful entry in the pipeline, and it is almost always nothing. Rackham's test is merciless: did the customer agree to do something specific, or only to continue being pleasant?

Once sellers were asked to plan an advance before every call and record whether they got one, their behaviour changed before anyone taught them anything new. And with a reliable definition of success, the researchers could go to the middle of the conversation and ask what the winners did there. They asked more questions.
ch.cap: Four stages, and an honest definition of progress

b: When customers talk about their problems they do it in two quite different registers, and the difference predicted everything. An implied need is a grumble. It is cumbersome. It is slower than I would like. An explicit need is a stated want. I need something faster. We have to cut that cost.

In small sales, implied needs predict the order. The more grumbles a seller collects, the more likely the sale. This is where most sales intuition comes from, because most salespeople cut their teeth on small sales. In large sales it stops working. The number of grumbles has little relationship to whether the customer buys. The number of explicit needs stated out loud has a strong one.

Underneath this sits what Rackham called the value equation, a balance with the seriousness of the problem on one side and the cost of the solution on the other. A small problem and a large price produce a no, however elegant the demonstration. The seller cannot change the price in the room. The seller can find out whether the problem is really as small as it first sounded.

That reframes the whole job. The questions are not there to qualify the customer, or to build rapport, or to fill the time before the pitch. The questions are the work. And here the data got slightly rude. Situation questions, the fact gathering openers about how many branches you have and what you use at the moment, were asked most by inexperienced sellers and least by top performers, and asking too many went with worse outcomes. Buyers resent being asked what the seller could have looked up.
ch.cap: A grumble is not the same as a want

b: Problem questions came next. Are you happy with your current arrangement, where does it let you down. These surface the grumbles, and in small sales they are strongly linked to success. In large sales they were necessary and not sufficient. The team found what was missing by looking at what good sellers did straight after a buyer admitted a problem. The average seller reached for the product. The successful seller stayed with the problem and followed it outwards. What does that delay cost you over a year, and what happens to your margins if it carries on?

Rackham called these implication questions, and they were the discovery of the project. Top performers asked roughly four times as many as average performers, and their use was strongly associated with success in large sales. They work by moving a problem from a nuisance the buyer has learned to live with into a cost he can see.

They are also the part that can be abused. An implication question makes the person you are talking to feel worse about their situation. Done honestly that is a service, because the cost was always there and they had stopped seeing it. Done to someone frightened or struggling, it manufactures distress in order to sell into it. The technique does not contain its ethics.

The fourth letter lifts the mood again. Need payoff questions ask about the value of a solution rather than the size of a problem. How would it help if you could do that? What would it be worth to your team? The buyer answers by describing the benefits in his own words, which is far stronger than hearing them stated at him. Situation, problem, implication, need payoff. The best salespeople were already doing it without knowing it had a name.
ch.cap: Following a problem out to its edges

b: The old training had a whole module on objection handling: learn the standard objections, rehearse the standard answers, treat an objection as a hurdle to be cleared with technique. The research turned this on its head. Successful salespeople did not handle objections better. They received fewer of them. Objections are mostly manufactured by the seller, and you can watch them being built, sentence by sentence, earlier in the same call.

The mechanism runs through features, advantages and benefits. A feature is a fact about the product, such as that it holds four hundred litres, and features are close to neutral. An advantage says what the product does for a customer in general: this will save you time. A benefit shows how it meets a need the buyer has already stated in their own words.

Advantages are the trap. In small sales they work perfectly well. In large sales they produce price objections, reliably and in proportion. The reason is almost arithmetic. Every time you describe a capability the buyer has not asked for, you add to the price in their head without adding to the problem. Tip that balance far enough and the buyer says, correctly, that this is more than they need and want to pay. The seller calls that an objection, when it was his own enthusiasm that produced it.

The last chapter is about how to learn any of this, and it is the least glamorous and most useful part. Expect to get worse before you get better. Practise one behaviour at a time. Try it at least three times before judging it, since the first attempt tells you only that it felt strange. Go for quantity before quality. And practise in safe situations, not in front of your largest customer.

b: By the middle of the 1980s Rackham had twelve years of data and a manuscript. Prentice Hall contracted the book and sent it to their expert reader for an opinion. The expert was a man called Roy Hall, and his review opened with a sentence Rackham has been quoting ever since. There is but one truth in this dungheap of words.

Hall's argument was not stupid. The book contradicted everything the field believed. It told salespeople that closing would hurt them, that talking about advantages would generate objections, and that the celebrated first ninety seconds barely mattered. Publishing it, Hall warned, would make the author a laughing stock.

Prentice Hall cancelled the contract. Rackham took the manuscript elsewhere and was turned down again, and again. Eight publishers saw it. McGraw Hill finally agreed, and only after he offered to buy back any copies unsold three months after publication.

It came out in 1988 and then did something books almost never do. It sold more every quarter for more than ten years, became a New York Times business bestseller, and has sold in the region of six million copies worldwide.

What carried it was not the writing, which is plain and repetitive by the author's own admission. It was adoption. Xerox went first, which mattered because everyone watched Xerox. IBM funded further research and put the model into several divisions. The delivery was unusual too: rather than flying in trainers, Huthwaite taught sales managers to code calls themselves, then had each coach three of their own people over three months.

b: Rackham led Huthwaite in the United States until 2003 and then became its strategic adviser. More books followed, and in 2006 he wrote Ending the War Between Sales and Marketing for the Harvard Business Review with Philip Kotler.

The second half of his life has been academic, with visiting professorships at Portsmouth, Cranfield, Cincinnati and Edinburgh Napier, and at Sheffield, where he started, since 2014. There he led researchers studying teamwork with behaviour analysis and artificial intelligence, the same tally sheet with better instruments.

Now the honest part. The research was commercial and proprietary. The headline numbers were never published in a journal where others could examine the coding scheme, the sampling or the statistics. Claims such as the one that the first thousand people trained outsold control groups by seventeen per cent cannot be checked. Treat the book as a very large private study by an interested party, which is not nothing and is not replicated science.

The model has been challenged too. In 2011 Matthew Dixon and Brent Adamson published The Challenger Sale, arguing from their own research that the relationship building salesperson was the weakest performer in complex sales, and that the strongest teach the customer something new. Rackham wrote its foreword. He did not defend his territory. He said buying had changed since the 1970s and selling needed a revolution to match it.

That response is the real lesson of his life, and it is worth more than the four letters. He had built a career on a model, and when better evidence arrived he treated it as interesting rather than threatening. Count what people actually do, compare it with what happened, and believe the count rather than the folklore, including your own.

connects: Claude Hopkins made advertising answerable to measured results rather than to taste; Rackham did the same thing to the sales conversation sixty years later, with a tally sheet instead of a coupon.
Chris Voss's calibrated questions do the same work as need payoff questions: they get the other side to state the case out loud in their own words rather than hearing it argued at them.
Dale Carnegie's advice to let the other person do most of the talking was folklore until Rackham's data showed that the people who ask more and talk less actually win more of the large sales.
note: Dates, roles and research figures come from Rackham's published biography and from the book itself, with the publication story and the Xerox funding account drawn from his own recorded interviews with Huthwaite International. Rackham is alive and his early life is barely documented beyond his schooling in Hampshire, a childhood partly spent in Borneo and his 1966 Sheffield degree, so the opening chapter stays with what is on the record rather than inventing a scene. The Huthwaite research was commercial and was never published in a peer reviewed journal, so the headline numbers, including the claim of seventeen per cent higher volume against control groups, cannot be independently verified. The Challenger Sale of 2011 directly challenged the consultative model, and Rackham wrote its foreword.
recall: What was the three to one observation that started Rackham's research?

A colleague pointed out that in most sales forces the top tenth of salespeople sold roughly three times what the bottom tenth sold, and that nobody knew why. Rackham treated that unexplained gap as a research question rather than a management problem.
What did the research find about closing techniques?

Closing techniques raised success rates in small, cheap sales and lowered them in large ones. A company selling both inexpensive and expensive products trained its people in closing and saw cheap sales rise while expensive sales fell.
What is the difference between an implied need and an explicit need?

An implied need is a grumble, such as saying a system is slow or awkward. An explicit need is a stated want, such as saying I need something faster. Implied needs predict small sales and explicit needs predict large ones.
Which of the four question types was the key discovery, and how much did top performers use it?

Implication questions, which follow a problem outwards into its costs and consequences. Top performers asked roughly four times as many of them as average performers, and their use was strongly linked to success in large sales.
What happened when Rackham first tried to publish the book?

Prentice Hall contracted it, then cancelled after its expert reader Roy Hall wrote a review beginning there is but one truth in this dungheap of words. Eight publishers saw the manuscript before McGraw Hill took it in 1988, and only after Rackham offered to buy back unsold copies.
recap:
Neil Rackham was an English psychologist, trained at Sheffield in the 1960s in a method called behaviour analysis, which means sitting in a room, categorising every single thing that is said, and refusing to draw conclusions the tally sheet does not support. A colleague told him that the best tenth of salespeople outsold the worst tenth by about three to one, and that nobody knew why. He decided to find out.

In 1974 he founded the Huthwaite Research Group, persuaded Xerox and later IBM to fund the work, and over about twelve years put roughly thirty researchers into something like thirty five thousand real sales calls across more than twenty countries. He went in expecting to find national styles of selling. He found instead that successful salespeople everywhere were doing the same things as one another.

Four findings came out of it. First, closing techniques raise success in small sales and lower it in large ones, because pressure applied to a big decision reads as a conflict of interest. Second, a successful call is not a pleasant one but one that ends in an order or an advance, meaning a specific agreed next action rather than a vague promise to stay in touch. Third, buyers talk about problems in two registers: implied needs, which are grumbles, and explicit needs, which are stated wants. Grumbles predict small sales and stated wants predict large ones. Fourth, objections are mostly manufactured by the seller, by describing capabilities the buyer never asked for and so adding price in their mind without adding value.

The method for getting from one to the other is the four letters. Situation questions, used sparingly. Problem questions, to surface the difficulty. Implication questions, which follow the problem out into what it costs, and which top performers used about four times as often as everyone else. And need payoff questions, which have the buyer describe the value of a solution in their own voice.

Prentice Hall's reader called the manuscript a dungheap of words and the contract was cancelled. Eight publishers refused it. It has since sold around six million copies, and when a rival model arrived in 2011 Rackham wrote its foreword rather than defending his own.

Ask more, pitch later, and believe the count rather than the folklore.
stories: One truth in this dungheap of words

In the middle 1980s Prentice Hall had Neil Rackham's manuscript under contract and sent it to their expert reader, Roy Hall. His review began: there is but one truth in this dungheap of words. Hall's point was that the book contradicted everything the profession believed, and that publishing it would make the author a laughing stock. The contract was cancelled. Eight publishers in total turned the manuscript down. McGraw Hill eventually agreed, but only after Rackham offered to buy back any copies still unsold three months after publication. It went on to sell about six million.

When Rackham entered the training industry around 1970, one widely taught sales course recommended roughly twenty short closing attempts in the course of a single sale. Another advised salespeople never to ask questions, on the grounds that a question gives the customer a chance to raise a doubt. His research found the opposite on both counts: in large sales, the more closing techniques used, the worse the call did, and the winners asked far more questions than the losers. The clearest proof came from a firm selling cheap and expensive items, where closing training raised one line and sank the other.
The European model that never existed

Rackham sold his study to Xerox partly on the promise of finding a distinctly European way of selling, arguing that the American methods being exported to Europe were built on American customer psychology. He fully expected the Scandinavians to sell differently from the southern Europeans. Across thirteen countries, the successful salespeople were doing the same things as one another, and the unsuccessful ones were making the same mistakes as one another. The hypothesis died and a much larger finding took its place: a good sales conversation appears to have a shape that survives language and culture.
take: A grumble is not a want
After a call, write down whether the customer complained about something or stated a thing they need. Only the second one predicts a decision worth having.
The bigger the commitment, the more a nudge reads as a conflict of interest. On any serious decision, replace urgency with clarity about what the problem is costing.
Before every important conversation, decide the specific next action you will ask for, then record whether you got it. A pleasant call with no agreed next step is a no wearing a smile.
Your own enthusiasm creates most objections
Every capability you describe that the customer never asked for adds price in their mind without adding value. Say less about the product until you know what they need it to do.
Questions are the work, not the warm up
Stop treating the fact find as something to get through before the pitch. The conversation is won in the middle, by what you ask and how far you follow it.
Do not ask what you could have looked up
Situation questions bore people and serve only you. Research first, then spend your questions on problems and consequences.
A reason the customer states in their own words is far stronger than the same reason delivered at them. Ask what it would be worth to them, then stop talking.
Believe the count over the lore
Whenever an industry has a confident explanation that nobody has measured, that is where the advantage is. Measure the thing yourself, even crudely.
title: The Man Who Sat In On Thirty Five Thousand Sales Calls
wiifm: Most of what you were taught about selling was invented by people who never measured anything. Rackham measured it, across thirty five thousand real conversations, and found that the sacred techniques work on small purchases and quietly destroy large ones. You run a business where the customer is putting their home against a loan and where the person on the phone can either serve them or hurry them. This gives you a tested, ethical shape for those conversations, a sharper definition of what a good call is, and a clear explanation of where price objections actually come from.
words: Based on what has been observed or measured rather than on theory or belief.
Rackham's whole contribution was to make selling an empirical subject, decided by tally sheets from real calls rather than by what trainers felt sure of.
